Green Chile Project | FERC Docket CP26-80-000


                                                   PUBLIC COMMENTS
                       Comments on the Environmental Assessment
              Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC - Green Chile Project | Docket No. CP26-80-000

Filed by                 Michael Gan, individual commenter
Date                     September 25, 2026

        I am submitting these comments regarding the Environmental Assessment (EA) prepared by Federal
   Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) staff for Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC's proposed Green
   Chile Project. I oppose authorization unless the record demonstrates that the project satisfies the Natural
   Gas Act's public-convenience-and-necessity standard and that the environmental, historic-preservation, and
   alternatives issues relevant to the pipeline have been adequately resolved.
       The public docket describes a project consisting of approximately 17.77 miles of new 24-inch-diameter
   natural-gas transmission pipeline, meter and regulator facilities, and appurtenances in Doña Ana County,
   New Mexico, with capacity to deliver up to 400,000 dekatherms per day. FERC's July 2026 schedule notice
   states that the project would deliver gas from the El Paso Natural Gas system to Green Chile Ventures, LLC,
   and that Transwestern says the gas would be used for power generation for a new artificial-intelligence/data-
   center campus.
   1. Project need and sizing under Natural Gas Act Section 7(e)
       Section 7(e) of the Natural Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. 717f(e), permits FERC to issue a certificate only when the
   proposed service, construction, or operation is or will be required by the present or future public convenience
   and necessity. FERC's 1999 Certificate Policy Statement, which the Commission has confirmed remains its
   operative framework, considers evidence of project need and balances public benefits against residual
   adverse effects.
         Because this project is designed to serve one identified new customer, the Commission's final order
   should identify the evidence supporting both the requested scale and the expected duration of need. The
   record should make clear the relevant service or precedent agreement, the contract term, projected
   utilization, whether the full 400,000 Dth/day capacity is subscribed or otherwise justified, and whether the
   proposed facilities are proportionate to demonstrated demand. A customer commitment can be important
   evidence of need, but the Commission should explain how that evidence supports the capacity and useful life
   of the facilities proposed here.
   2. Reasonable alternatives and project configuration
       FERC's Notice of Availability states that the EA is intended to identify and assess environmental effects,
   describe and evaluate reasonable alternatives, and identify mitigation measures. In the final record, the
   Commission should clearly explain the disposition of reasonable lower-impact alternatives, including whether
   existing pipeline capacity, a smaller-capacity lateral, route modifications, or other technically feasible
   configurations could meet the demonstrated need with less land disturbance or fewer adverse effects.
       I am not asserting that the EA omitted a particular alternative that I have not independently verified.
   Rather, I ask the Commission to make the alternatives analysis and its connection to the final certificate
   decision clear enough for the public record to show why the selected configuration is warranted.
   3. Historic and cultural resources
        This project's procedural history makes historic-preservation review particularly important. On April 13,
   2026, FERC staff protested Transwestern's original blanket-certificate prior-notice request because the
   record did not include a New Mexico State Historic Preservation Office finding of "no historic properties" or
   "no historic properties affected." FERC's July 2026 schedule notice states that the documentation was not
   filed by the applicable deadline and that the request therefore proceeded as an application for case-specific
   authorization under Section 7 of the NGA pursuant to 18 CFR 157.205(f).
       Before issuing any certificate, the Commission should clearly identify the current status of the Section
   106 process, relevant SHPO and Tribal consultation, affected historic properties if any, and any enforceable
   avoidance, mitigation, monitoring, or unanticipated-discovery requirements. If consultation or documentation
   remains incomplete, the certificate decision should not assume a completed record.




                                                           Page 1
                                    Green Chile Project | FERC Docket CP26-80-000


4. Pipeline-specific environmental effects, mitigation, and monitoring
     For the pipeline itself, the final decision should clearly state how FERC evaluated construction and
operational effects involving land disturbance, water resources, wildlife and habitat, air emissions and fugitive
methane, restoration, and long-term right-of-way maintenance. Where the Commission relies on mitigation to
support its environmental conclusions, the record should identify the measures relied upon, the responsible
party, applicable monitoring or reporting, and whether those measures are incorporated as enforceable
certificate conditions.
    The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) previously issued a right-of-way decision for approximately 16
miles of the pipeline across BLM-administered land and later participated as a cooperating agency in FERC's
EA. That earlier record is relevant, but FERC remains responsible for its own Section 7 certificate decision
and NEPA record. The Commission should explain how it used BLM's prior analysis and which project-
specific findings or conditions it independently adopts.
5. Relationship to the data-center campus
     I recognize that the associated data-center campus is a separate project outside FERC's direct pipeline
jurisdiction. In Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168 (2025), the Supreme
Court held that NEPA does not necessarily require an agency to analyze environmental consequences of a
separate upstream or downstream project merely because the federal action facilitates it, particularly when
that separate project lies outside the agency's regulatory authority. I therefore am not asking FERC to
regulate the data center's overall water use, electricity policy, or other matters beyond FERC's authority.
     The data center remains directly relevant to a different question: project need. It is the stated reason for
this pipeline. The Commission should therefore explain the evidence supporting the customer's projected gas
demand, timing, duration, and utilization when determining whether the proposed pipeline capacity is
required by the public convenience and necessity. The final order should distinguish that NGA need inquiry
from the separate question of which environmental effects are legally attributable to the pipeline for NEPA
purposes.
6. Related infrastructure and completeness of the final record
    The final record should also identify the geographic and temporal scope of any applicable cumulative-
effects or related-infrastructure analysis and explain which related natural-gas facilities or federal actions
were considered. This request is not intended to expand NEPA beyond current law; it is intended to make
clear what the Commission considered and why, particularly where other facilities or federal authorizations
bear directly on the pipeline's construction, operation, or environmental effects.
Conclusion
     For these reasons, I ask FERC not to authorize the Green Chile Project unless the record demonstrates
a need commensurate with the project's scale, completes the applicable historic-preservation process,
adequately evaluates reasonable alternatives, and supports its environmental conclusions with enforceable
mitigation where necessary. If material issues remain unresolved, the Commission should defer authorization
until the record is complete.
    A separate supplement, Selected Legal, Agency, and Technical References, identifies the principal
statutory, agency, judicial, and project-record sources supporting these comments and frames unresolved
matters as questions for the Commission's final record rather than as unverified assertions about the EA.

Respectfully submitted,
Michael Gan
Individual commenter

                         Selected Legal, Agency, and Technical References

                                  Green Chile Project - FERC Docket No. CP26-80-000
                    Supplement to public comments on the Environmental Assessment | September 2026

Purpose and scope. This supplement identifies confirmed facts in the public docket, the principal statutory and policy
standards governing FERC's certificate decision, and targeted questions for the Commission's final record. It does not
assert that an issue was omitted from the Environmental Assessment unless the cited public record establishes that
omission.



1. Confirmed project and procedural record

2. Governing certificate standard and current FERC policy
Natural Gas Act Section 7(e), 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e). FERC may issue a certificate only if the applicant is able and willing to
comply with applicable requirements and the proposed service, construction, or operation is or will be required by the
present or future public convenience and necessity. Otherwise, the application is to be denied. FERC may impose
reasonable certificate conditions.
1999 Certificate Policy Statement, PL99-3-000. FERC's 1999 policy states that it considers relevant evidence of project
need and balances public benefits against residual adverse effects. It identifies evidence such as precedent agreements,
demand projections, potential consumer savings, and comparisons of projected demand with existing capacity. It also
emphasizes avoiding unnecessary overbuilding, environmental disruption, and unneeded exercise of eminent domain.
Current status of the 1999 framework. In September 2025, FERC terminated the draft Updated Certificate Policy
Statement proceeding and stated that the 1999 Certificate Policy Statement continues to provide the appropriate
framework for proposed natural-gas projects. A March 2026 FERC order likewise describes the operative sequence: no
                                                           Page 1
                                                                                         Green Chile Project | FERC Docket CP26-80-000
subsidization by existing customers; efforts to eliminate or minimize adverse effects; balancing residual adverse effects
against public benefits; and then completion of environmental review.
NEPA scope after Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, 605 U.S. 168 (2025). The Supreme Court
held that NEPA does not necessarily require an agency to analyze environmental effects of a separate upstream or
downstream project merely because the federal project may facilitate it, particularly where the separate project is outside
the agency's regulatory authority. The Court also distinguished those separate-project effects from indirect effects of the
federal project itself, which can remain within NEPA's scope.



3. Issues that merit a clear Commission response
   Demonstrated need and sizing: Because the project is designed for one identified new customer and a stated
    maximum delivery of 400,000 Dth/day, the Commission should identify the evidence supporting the amount and
    expected duration of demand. The record should make clear the relevant service or precedent agreement, contract
    term, expected utilization, whether the full capacity is subscribed or otherwise justified, and whether the proposed
    scale is proportionate to demonstrated need.
   Existing capacity and reasonable alternatives: FERC's EA notice specifically asks commenters to address
    reasonable alternatives. The final record should clearly explain whether existing pipeline capacity, a smaller-capacity
    lateral, route modifications, or other technically feasible configurations could meet the demonstrated need with less
    land disturbance or fewer adverse effects.
   Historic and cultural resources: The April staff protest establishes that required New Mexico SHPO documentation
    was absent at that stage. Before a certificate is issued, the final record should identify the current Section 106 status,
    any SHPO and Tribal consultation relevant to the undertaking, affected historic properties if any, and enforceable
    avoidance, mitigation, monitoring, and unanticipated-discovery requirements.
   Pipeline-specific environmental effects: The Commission should clearly explain its treatment of effects attributable
    to construction and operation of the pipeline itself, including land disturbance, water resources, wildlife and habitat,
    air emissions, fugitive methane, restoration, and long-term right-of-way maintenance, together with the mitigation
    and monitoring relied upon in reaching any significance determination.
   Relationship to the data-center campus: The separate data-center campus is described by FERC as non-
    jurisdictional, and current NEPA law does not necessarily require FERC to evaluate every environmental effect of that
    separate project. However, the campus's demand is the stated reason for the pipeline. The Commission can therefore
    distinguish two questions: (1) what evidence of the customer's demand supports the NGA need determination; and (2)
    which environmental consequences are legally attributable to the pipeline itself for NEPA purposes.
   Cumulative and related infrastructure: The final record should identify the geographic and temporal scope used
    for any cumulative-effects analysis that remains applicable under current NEPA law, and explain which related
    natural-gas facilities or federal actions were considered and why.
   BLM's prior right-of-way decision: BLM's May 2026 EA and right-of-way record are relevant agency materials, but
    FERC remains responsible for its independent Natural Gas Act certificate decision and its own NEPA record. The
    Commission should explain how it used BLM's analysis and which project-specific findings or conditions it
    independently adopts.
